siteTitle: The Current War | Film & Technology Analysis

partitions.heading: The Current War: Director's Cut (2019)
partitions.subtitle: Film Critique & 2nd Industrial Revolution Assessment by Aloysius Conway

cards.title: Historical Scope & Core Thesis
cards.text: Alfonso Gomez-Rejon's 'The Current War' dramatizes the high-stakes clash between Thomas Edison, George Westinghouse, and Nikola Tesla. This historical fight was fought to determine whether direct current (DC) or alternating current (AC) would become the foundational standard for America's future power grid. While popular culture often remembers Edison as an untouchable hero of invention, the film presents a grounded and human look at how industrial ambition, patent wars, and public relations shaped the modern electrical age.

partitions.heading: The Film Breakdown (SUPER SPOILER EDITION)
partitions.subtitle: How a Personal Rivalry Decided the Standard for America's Power Grid

cards.title: Act I: A Spurned Invitation and the Flaws of Direct Current
cards.text: After Thomas Edison illuminates lower Manhattan with direct current, Pittsburgh industrialist George Westinghouse invites Edison to a formal dinner to propose an alliance. Edison spurns the invitation and orders his train to bypass the station as Westinghouse waits on the platform. Offended by the slight, Westinghouse begins studying electrical distribution on his own. He soon realizes that Edison's DC system has severe distance limits that make it impractical for nationwide expansion, setting the stage for an intense fight to prove alternating current is the superior path for the future.

cards.title: Act II: Tesla's Struggle and the AC Alliance
cards.text: Nikola Tesla arrives in New York eager to work for Edison and proposes that alternating current can carry electricity over hundreds of miles. Edison dismisses Tesla's ideas as dangerous and refuses to pay him promised bonuses. Tesla resigns in frustration and falls into deep poverty, eventually digging ditches just to survive. Westinghouse eventually tracks Tesla down and purchases his alternating current patents, giving Westinghouse the working motor he needs to take on Edison's electrical empire.

cards.title: Act III: The Chicago World's Fair and the Defeat of Edison
cards.text: The competition reaches its climax in the bidding war to power the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. When Edison uses patent lawsuits to block Westinghouse from using his light bulbs, Westinghouse bypasses the obstacle by engineering the two-piece stopper bulb. Westinghouse underbids Edison, lights the fair with thousands of alternating current lamps without a single failure, and secures the landmark contract at Niagara Falls. Edison is pushed out of his own electrical business as J.P. Morgan consolidates the company into General Electric.

cards.text: The official theatrical trailer highlights the film's visual approach and captures the central conflict between Benedict Cumberbatch as Edison, Michael Shannon as Westinghouse, and Nicholas Hoult as Tesla.

partitions.heading: Cast, Filmmakers & Character Dynamics
partitions.subtitle: Performances That Humanize Gilded Age Titans

cards.title: Director: Alfonso Gomez-Rejon
cards.text: Director Alfonso Gomez-Rejon gives this historical drama a fast and energetic style by relying on Dutch angles, tracking shots, and strong lighting contrast to reflect the themes of electricity. The movie was shelved in 2017 during the collapse of The Weinstein Company, but Gomez-Rejon eventually regained control to film pick-up scenes and release his true Director's Cut in 2019.

cards.title: Lead Cast & Character Portrayals
cards.text: Benedict Cumberbatch plays Edison as an obstinate and proud innovator whose public image matters as much as his work. Michael Shannon brings a quiet and principled presence to George Westinghouse, making him a steady counterweight to Edison. Nicholas Hoult highlights Tesla's technical brilliance alongside his social isolation, and Tom Holland plays Samuel Insull, Edison's loyal assistant who watches the business slip away.

partitions.heading: Technologies of the 2nd Industrial Revolution
partitions.subtitle: The Inventions That Decided America's Energy and Media Infrastructure

cards.title: 1. Direct Current (DC) vs. Alternating Current (AC) Transmission
cards.text: Edison's direct current system operated at low household voltages around 110 volts. Because transmitting high power at low voltage requires massive electric current, Edison's lines suffered from heavy resistive heat loss (P = I²R). Thick copper conductors were required, and generation stations had to be built every mile. Alternating current solved this limitation by using step-up transformers to boost voltage into the thousands. This allowed electricity to travel over long distances through thinner wires before step-down transformers reduced the voltage safely for homes.
points: DC: Low voltage, high current, heavy copper cables, and a one-mile transmission limit.
AC: High-voltage transmission, smaller conductors, and long-range power delivery from central plants.
Historical Significance: This physical difference made AC the practical foundation for the modern national grid.

cards.title: 2. Tesla's Polyphase AC Induction Motor
cards.text: Before Tesla's breakthrough, alternating current had one glaring flaw: there was no practical motor that could run on it. Direct current motors relied on mechanical brushes and commutators that wore out quickly and generated dangerous sparks. Tesla designed an induction motor that utilized alternating polyphase currents to produce a rotating magnetic field. This allowed a rotor to turn entirely through magnetic induction without any mechanical brushes, providing the durable industrial motor that AC needed to power factories and transit systems.

cards.title: 3. Edison's Incandescent Light Bulb
cards.text: Thomas Edison did not create the first light bulb, but he perfected the first commercially viable incandescent system. He developed a high-resistance carbonized bamboo filament enclosed in an evacuated glass bulb with a standardized screw base. This high resistance allowed bulbs to run efficiently in parallel circuits so that one burned-out lamp did not shut off the rest of the building.

cards.title: 4. Westinghouse's Stopper Bulb Solution
cards.text: When Westinghouse won the contract to illuminate the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, Edison secured a court injunction forbidding Westinghouse from using Edison's patented one-piece fused glass bulb. To avoid a massive financial disaster, Westinghouse acquired the Sawyer-Man lamp patents and manufactured the 'stopper bulb.' This design featured a two-piece glass body sealed with a ground-glass plug and used cheaper iron lead wires, allowing Westinghouse to supply almost 100,000 bulbs without infringing on Edison's patents.

cards.title: 5. Edison's Wax Cylinder Phonograph
cards.text: As the corporate battle dragged on, Edison turned back to his earlier breakthroughs to keep his laboratory funded. The phonograph recorded sound waves by indenting physical grooves onto a rotating tinfoil or wax cylinder with a vibrating stylus, then played the audio back through a mechanical diaphragm and horn. The film shows this device in an intimate moment where Edison records his dying wife Mary so he can preserve her voice.

cards.title: 6. The Kinetograph and Kinetoscope (Early Motion Pictures)
cards.text: Toward the end of the film at the Chicago World's Fair, Edison realizes that alternating current has won the electrical war. Instead of admitting complete defeat, he shifts his creative energy toward motion pictures. Edison shows Westinghouse a strip of perforated celluloid film and explains his work on the Kinetograph camera and Kinetoscope peep-hole viewer, remarking that moving pictures would become so significant that people would eventually forget he ever worked on electricity.

cards.title: 7. The Electric Chair and the Smear Campaign
cards.text: In a bid to frighten the public away from alternating current, Edison covertly funded engineer Harold P. Brown to hold public animal electrocution demonstrations. Edison then secretly helped arrange for Westinghouse AC generators to be installed at Auburn Prison for the 1890 execution of William Kemmler, hoping people would associate AC with sudden death and start calling electrocution being 'Westinghoused.' The resulting botched execution horrified the public and damaged Edison's moral reputation.

partitions.heading: Critique, Historical Accuracy & Reception
partitions.subtitle: Separating Hollywood Drama from Historical Truth

cards.title: Student Film Review
cards.text: 'The Current War' avoids standard movie cliches by showing both Edison and Westinghouse as complex men driven by personal ambition and corporate survival. Michael Shannon gives Westinghouse a calm and dignified presence that anchors the story, balancing Benedict Cumberbatch's portrayal of Edison as a frantic and stubborn visionary. The film does an excellent job of turning complex engineering principles and business deals into an engaging story.

cards.title: Historical Accuracy vs. Dramatic License
cards.text: The film gets the science and corporate rivalry right, but it takes several dramatic liberties with real history. Thomas Edison and George Westinghouse never had a direct conversation in real life, meaning their climactic dialogue at the Chicago World's Fair was invented by the writers to give the rivalry emotional closure. Additionally, Edison had already been forced out of Edison General Electric before the fair opened, after J.P. Morgan orchestrated the merger that created General Electric.
